title: Louisville & Nashville Railroad opens the interior
summary: The Louisville and Nashville Railroad, finished in 1859, linked Louisville with Nashville and opened Kentucky's interior to year-round trade.
bodyMarkdown:
The Louisville & Nashville Railroad, the L&N, began as a line between two river cities and grew into one of the great railroads of the South. Along the way it opened Kentucky's coalfields and tied the state to Gulf ports. It ran under the same name for 132 years.

## Charter and construction

According to the [L&N Historical Society's history](https://www.lnrr.org/History.aspx) by Charles B. Castner, Kentucky chartered the company on March 5, 1850. The charter allowed a line from Louisville to the Tennessee state line "in the direction of Nashville." On December 4, 1851, Tennessee authorized the extension to Nashville.

Track laying began at Ninth Street and Broadway in Louisville in May 1853. By 1855 the founders, mostly Louisville citizens, had raised nearly $3 million. On August 25, 1855, the first train carried about 300 people eight miles out of Louisville at 15 miles per hour.

On October 27, 1859, the first train ran the whole way from Louisville to Nashville. The society gives the line's length as 187 miles and its cost as $7,221,204.91. Scheduled trains began a few days later.

## War and growth

By 1861 the L&N had 269 miles of track. Lying between the two armies, it served both the Union and the Confederacy at different times and suffered considerable damage. An account of [Louisville and Nashville Railroad](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louisville_and_Nashville_Railroad) says its war work also brought profits. The company came out of the war in good financial shape and began to expand.

Within about 30 years the L&N reached St. Louis, Cincinnati, Memphis, Birmingham, Mobile, Pensacola and New Orleans. It reached the Gulf ports in 1881. Under Milton H. Smith, president for nearly 40 years, it grew into a major railroad system. In the 1880s and 1890s it acquired, leased or built 56 railroads.

## Into the coalfields

Between 1879 and 1881 the L&N bought track that gave it access to the western Kentucky coalfields. In 1881 it began extending its Lebanon Branch across the Tennessee line to Jellico. In 1909 it bought two smaller lines, and in 1911 and 1912 it built more than 150 miles of track along the Cumberland River and the North Fork of the Kentucky River. These lines reached the coalfields around Hazard and Harlan in eastern Kentucky.

Its reliable service earned it the nickname "The Old Reliable."

## Kentucky today

The Seaboard Coast Line bought the rest of the L&N's stock in 1971, and the L&N was merged out of existence at the end of 1982. CSX now owns and runs the former L&N lines that were not abandoned or sold. [L&N collections](https://grokipedia.com/page/Louisville_and_Nashville_Railroad) are kept at the Kentucky Railway Museum in New Haven and the Historic RailPark and Train Museum in Bowling Green.

For an earlier Kentucky line, see the [Lexington and Ohio Railroad](/stories/lexington-ohio-railroad/). For the road-building fight before it, see [the Maysville Road veto](/stories/the-maysville-road-and-jacksons-veto-1830/).
